assessment: The Medellín article used cinnamon as a diagnostic odor and gives a separate recognition count. No ingestion was tested. This is the same study as W7207332803. See research/2020-2024/Food-Experiment-Evidence.md#cinnamon-odor-identification-in-the-medellín-clinic.

The publisher's text discusses alertness and fatigue for methylxanthines generally and Parkinson diagnosis risk separately. It gives no brewed coffee and fatigue comparison in Parkinson disease. DOI 10.29057/icsa.v6i12.3099.

The Universidad de Antioquia thesis describes the same diagnostic odor study as W4405588914. Cinnamon was smelled. See research/2020-2024/Food-Experiment-Evidence.md#cinnamon-odor-identification-in-the-medellín-clinic.

Cinnamon was one of 12 odor pens in the Chilean study. The report compares aggregate scores by diagnostic group and gives no cinnamon-specific outcome or ingestion result. See research/2005-2009/Food-Experiment-Multilingual-Followup.md#2006-chilean-food-odor-recognition-test.

The deposited full report discusses fatigue effects of caffeine generally. Parkinson disease appears separately in a summary of disease risk. It reports no measured fatigue contrast in a Parkinson sample. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.7930395.

The thesis injected hydroxytyrosol in MPP+ rats. Locomotor counts did not clearly differ, and the report measures forced swimming and drug-induced rotations. It does not test edible oil, rest tremor or bradykinesia. See research/2015-2019/Food-Experiment-Spanish-Context-Followup.md#intravenous-hydroxytyrosol-and-movement-in-a-rat-model.
The bilingual pharmaceutical dictionary covers a range of nutrition and drug topics. The indexed record supplies no studied population, ingredient assignment or Parkinson outcome.

The University of Distrital thesis studies plant transcripts. Banana appears in a cannabis cultivar name and anxiety in general use background. It reports no banana consumption or measured Parkinson symptom. Repository handle 11349/6589.
